The Vital Conditions framework

Seven conditions every community needs to be healthy, from the Well Being In the Nation (WIN) network. Each card below shows its ACS proxy metric(s), where one exists.

Basic Needs for Health + Safety

Basic requirements for health and safety

Nutritious food, safe drinking water, fresh air, sufficient sleep, routine physical activity, safe sexuality and reproduction, freedom from trauma/violence/addiction/crime, routine physical and behavioral health care

Humane Housing

Humane, consistent housing

Adequate space per person; safe structures; affordable costs; diverse neighborhoods (without gentrification, segregation, concentrated poverty); close to work, school, food, recreation, and nature

Meaningful Work + Wealth

Rewarding work, careers, and standards of living

Job training/retraining; good-paying and fulfilling jobs; family and community wealth; savings and limited debt

Lifelong Learning

Continuous learning, education, and literacy

Continuous development of cognitive, social, emotional abilities; early childhood experiences; elementary, high school, and higher education; career and adult education

Reliable Transportation

Reliable, safe, and accessible transportation

Close to work, school, food, leisure; safe transport; active transport; efficient energy use; few environmental hazards

Belonging + Civic Muscle

Sense of belonging and power to shape a common world

Social support; freedom from stigma, discrimination, oppression; arts, culture, and spiritual life; organizing, advocacy, leadership development; civic agency; equitable access to information, communications, and technology; welcoming, inclusive places; opportunities for civic engagement

no ACS data

Thriving Natural World

Sustainable resources, contact with nature, freedom from hazards

Clean air, water, soil; healthy ecosystems; accessible natural spaces; freedom from extreme heat, flooding, wind, radiation, earthquakes, pathogens

Thriving Natural World has no ACS Data Profile equivalent -- clean air/water, natural hazards, and ecosystem health come from EPA/FEMA sources, not a household survey. It's included above for framework completeness but isn't charted below.

Understanding these numbers

What does "±" mean, and why does it matter?

These estimates come from the American Community Survey, which asks a sample of households each year -- not every household. Because it's a sample, every number here is an estimate with some built-in uncertainty, not an exact head-count.

The ± number next to an estimate is its margin of error (MOE). It's the range the true value most likely falls in. For example, "10.2% ± 0.7%" means the real figure is probably somewhere between 9.5% and 10.9% -- not exactly 10.2%.

Why be cautious: smaller counties and smaller population groups get surveyed less, so their estimates carry wider margins of error -- less precision. The colored dot next to each number flags how much to trust it:

  • reliable margin of error is small; treat the number as fairly precise.
  • caution margin of error is sizeable; treat the number as approximate.
  • unreliable margin of error is very large; treat the number as a rough signal, not a fact.

Rule of thumb: if two counties' ranges (value ± MOE) overlap, don't assume one is really higher or lower than the other -- the difference could just be survey noise. Hover any ± number or dot throughout this report for a plain-language explanation of that specific value.

Veteran vs. civilian comparison (2024)

Focus counties. ACS only cross-tabulates a handful of things by veteran status: poverty, unemployment, personal income, and educational attainment below, plus veteran-only service-connected disability rating. It does not break out health insurance, housing cost burden, vehicle access, commute time, or broadband access by veteran status -- those vital-conditions metrics above are population-wide only, with no veteran-specific split available anywhere in ACS.
